transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, um... I guess my primary care doctor suggested I come in, but really, it all stems from this... this ongoing situation at work that is just completely consuming my life right now. I’m a translator and an interpreter, mostly handling very dense technical and legal documents. I have my master's degree, I’ve been doing this for over fifteen years, so I am extremely meticulous. I have to be. 

But for months now—literally going back to at least October—I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in our project files. It’s not a coincidence, and it’s... it's incredibly frustrating to deal with day in and day out. See, we use this specialized localization software that relies on what we call a translation memory, or a TM, which basically stores previously translated segments so we maintain consistency across large projects. But certain subcontractors

When you think about this pattern with the subcontractors, do you ever consider that there might be another explanation—like a technical glitch or misunderstanding—or are you completely certain that this is intentional sabotage?

A technical glitch? No, see, I—I understand why you might ask that, because to an outsider, localization software can seem incredibly complex, and sure, glitches happen. I’ve been doing this for fifteen years, so I know exactly what a software bug looks like. A bug is random. A bug drops a formatting tag or corrupts a file extension. What I am dealing with... what is happening here is so meticulously targeted, it completely defies the logic of a simple glitch or a misunderstanding. 

I have thought about every possible angle, but for months now, I’ve been tracking this pattern in the project files, and it is deliberate. It’s certain subcontractors, yes, but there is also one colleague in particular—an in-house reviewer—who is absolutely involved in this. They are going into the translation memory database and making these tiny, almost microscopic changes. We're talking about shifting a comma, changing a passive voice to active in a dense legal clause, altering a standardized glossary term just enough that it triggers a critical error in the final QA check. 

And the most insidious part is the timing. They are manipulating the timestamps. So, when the final export is generated for the client, the system logs show that *I* was the last one to touch the segment. It is perfectly orchestrated so it looks exactly like my quality control failed. Like I’m slipping, like I don't know how to do my job anymore. 

And I know what people say—I went directly to our IT department about this, because obviously you need digital proof. I had them pull the server logs. But whoever is doing this, this colleague, they know exactly how to cover their tracks. IT came back to me and said the audit trail is clean, that there's no evidence of unauthorized access or tampering. But IT doesn't understand the linguistic nuances of a TM! They just look at ones and zeros, they don't see the context. Just because the audit trail looks clean to a network tech doesn't mean it wasn't manipulated. I know—I am completely, one hundred percent certain—that the record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame squarely on me. It’s a coordinated effort to ruin my professional reputation, and it’s just exhausting having to defend myself against something so calculated.
Aside from this situation at work, have you noticed similar feelings of being deliberately targeted or sabotaged by other people in your personal life, such as friends or family?

No, no, not at all. It’s strictly... it’s entirely confined to this specific professional environment. My personal life is—well, it's perfectly normal, actually. I mean, my wife and I have our usual routines, we still do our Sunday dinners, I help the kids with their homework—especially their language arts, obviously. And even at work, honestly, outside of this specific project issue with the translation memory, I’m still functioning at a very high level. I still handle all my regular translation duties, I manage my team’s workflow, I coordinate with the vendors, I make sure the invoices are paid on time... all of that is running like clockwork. 

It’s really just... the only time things go off track, the only time I feel this intense pressure and frustration, is when the file history comes up, or when I have to interact with those specific coworkers who I know are involved in this. It’s like a switch flips, because I know what they’re doing behind the scenes. But outside of that very specific context? No, my friends aren't plotting against me, my family isn't sabotaging me. It’s not paranoia, Doctor. It’s just this one, highly coordinated effort to undermine my work on this particular account. Everything else in my life is completely fine.

latest_inference.note: Patient describes a fixed, systematized, non-bizarre persecutory belief (colleague deliberately altering TM records and manipulating timestamps) that has persisted for months, is impervious to contrary evidence (clean IT audit trail), yet is encapsulated strictly to this one work scenario. Functioning outside this specific belief—family life, other work duties—remains fully intact, arguing against a broader stress/adjustment reaction (F43.2) or pervasive personality pathology (F60.5). This pattern of a single, well-organized, persistent delusion without other psychotic symptoms or global functional decline is most consistent with Delusional Disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion—that a colleague is deliberately manipulating translation memory records and timestamps to sabotage his work—held with complete conviction despite contradictory evidence (clean IT audit trail). The belief is systematized, encapsulated to one specific professional context, and has persisted for several months (since at least October). Notably, there are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or behavior, no negative symptoms, and no mood episode symptoms. Functioning is well preserved in all other domains (family life, most work duties, social relationships), which is inconsistent with schizophrenia (which typically causes broader deterioration) and more consistent with Delusional Disorder. The circumscribed, non-bizarre nature of the delusion and preserved global functioning support F22 over F20.0 (paranoid schizophrenia) or F28 (other psychotic disorder).
